title: ESXi Virtual Machine Snapshots Deleted via API
description: Detects removal of one or more virtual machine snapshots on a VMware ESXi host through a direct VIM API call (e.g. RemoveSnapshot_Task / RemoveAllSnapshots_Task), such as those issued by PowerCLI, govc, pyVmomi scripts, or any custom SOAP/REST client talking to hostd. Ransomware operators who have obtained ESXi credentials or a stolen vCenter/SSO session frequently delete every recoverable snapshot immediately before encrypting .vmdk files, so the victim cannot roll back instead of paying.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Records the VIM API task lifecycle for every snapshot operation (Task Created / Task Completed) including the sub=Vimsvc.TaskManager entry, the invoking user/session, and the target VM's vim.VirtualMachine MoRef.

data_sources.name: vpxd.log / vCenter Events
data_sources.description: If the host is managed by vCenter, VmRemoveAllSnapshotsEvent / VmRemoveSnapshotEvent appear in the Events table with full user attribution, which is far more reliable than hostd.log alone.

detection_logic: Search VMware task/event data for RemoveSnapshot_Task or RemoveAllSnapshots_Task completions, or the equivalent VmRemoveSnapshotEvent/VmRemoveAllSnapshotsEvent from vCenter, and alert when they occur outside of change windows, in a burst across multiple VMs, or are issued by an account that does not normally manage snapshots (e.g. root, a break-glass account, or a newly created SSO user).
spl:
index=vmware sourcetype=vmware:vc:events (eventtype=VmRemoveAllSnapshotsEvent OR eventtype=VmRemoveSnapshotEvent)
| stats count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(vm) as vms_affected by user, esxi_host
| where count >= 1
| eval risk_note=if(count>=3,"Bulk snapshot deletion across multiple VMs - high-confidence ransomware precursor","Single snapshot deletion - verify against change ticket")
cli_reference: vSphere API: VirtualMachineSnapshot.RemoveSnapshot_Task / VirtualMachine.RemoveAllSnapshots_Task (commonly invoked via PowerCLI Remove-Snapshot, govc snapshot.remove, or pyVmomi)
how_to_implement: Forward hostd.log to your SIEM via esxcli system syslog config set --loghost=<collector>, and/or ingest vCenter Server task/event data (Splunk Add-on for VMware, vRealize Log Insight, or the vSphere Events API) so deletions are attributed to a real user identity rather than just 'root' on the host.
known_false_positives: Legitimate backup software (Veeam, Commvault, etc.) creates and removes snapshots as part of normal backup jobs and can trigger this at scale; baseline your backup service accounts and exclude their known job windows.
investigation_steps: Identify the authenticated user/session and source IP that issued the task in vCenter events or the hostd opID.
Determine whether the account is a known backup/orchestration service account with an expected job schedule.
Check for correlated activity on the same host: VM power-off, autostart changes, firewall/coredump changes, or new SSH sessions in the same time window.
Verify whether any VM files (.vmdk, .vmx) were modified or renamed immediately afterward, which would indicate active encryption.

references.title: CISA AA23-039A: ESXiArgs Ransomware Virtual Machine Recovery Guidance
VMware Security Blog: ESXi-Targeting Ransomware, Tactics and Techniques

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi Autostart Settings Modified via API
description: Detects changes to a host's virtual machine AutoStart/AutoStop defaults or per-VM autostart entries made through the vSphere API (HostAutoStartManager.ReconfigureAutostart / UpdateDefaults / UpdateAutoStartEntry). Attackers disable autostart so that, after powering off VMs or rebooting the host, workloads do not automatically resume and expose the still-unencrypted disks - or, inversely, so a malicious VM they planted starts automatically on boot.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Logs HostAutoStartManager.ReconfigureAutostart / UpdateDefaults / UpdateAutoStartEntry task creation and completion with the invoking session.

data_sources.name: vCenter Events
data_sources.description: HostAutoStartConfiguredForVM style entries when driven through vCenter.

detection_logic: Alert on HostAutoStartManager reconfiguration tasks, especially those that set the global 'enabled' default to false or change per-VM startAction/waitForHeartbeat entries to 'none', outside of documented maintenance windows.
spl:
index=vmware sourcetype=vmware:esxi:hostd sub="Vimsvc.TaskManager" ("HostAutoStartManager.ReconfigureAutostart" OR "UpdateAutoStartEntry" OR "UpdateDefaults")
| rex field=_raw "user=(?<user>[^\]\s]+)"
| stats count values(_raw) as evidence by user, host
| where count > 0
cli_reference: vSphere API: HostAutoStartManager.ReconfigureAutostart / UpdateDefaults / UpdateAutoStartEntry (commonly invoked via PowerCLI Set-VMHostStartPolicy or govc host.autostart.*)
how_to_implement: Ensure hostd.log is forwarded and, where possible, correlate with vCenter's HostConfigChangedEvent so the responsible identity is captured rather than just 'root' on the host.
known_false_positives: Legitimate infrastructure automation (Ansible, Terraform vsphere provider, cluster build-out scripts) commonly configures autostart during host provisioning; baseline expected change windows and CMDB-registered automation accounts.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether the change is tied to a documented provisioning or DR runbook.
Check whether the 'enabled' default flipped from true to false, or whether specific high-value VMs were pulled out of the autostart list.
Correlate with subsequent VM power-off or snapshot-deletion events on the same host.

references.title: Broadcom TechDocs: Configure Virtual Machine Startup and Shutdown Settings

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi Virtual Machine Powered Off via ESXi API
description: Detects one or more virtual machines being powered off through the vSphere API (VirtualMachine.PowerOffVM_Task) rather than through in-guest shutdown. Encryptors used by ESXi-targeting ransomware families (e.g. LockBit, Black Basta, Akira, RansomHub) power off every running VM first to release the .vmdk file locks held by the running VMX process, which is a prerequisite for encrypting the files.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Logs PowerOffVM_Task creation/completion for each VM MoRef.

data_sources.name: vobd.log
data_sources.description: Emits VM power-state VOB observations that can corroborate a mass power-off independent of hostd.

data_sources.name: vCenter Events
data_sources.description: VmPoweredOffEvent with reliable user attribution when the host is vCenter-managed.

detection_logic: Count distinct VmPoweredOffEvent / PowerOffVM_Task occurrences per host per short rolling window (e.g. 5 minutes). More than a handful of VMs powering off together, especially initiated by the same session, is a strong ransomware-staging indicator rather than routine admin work.
spl:
index=vmware sourcetype=vmware:vc:events eventtype=VmPoweredOffEvent
| bucket _time span=5m
| stats dc(vm) as vms_powered_off values(vm) as vm_list by _time, user, esxi_host
| where vms_powered_off >= 5
| eval alert="Mass VM power-off - possible ransomware staging"
cli_reference: vSphere API: VirtualMachine.PowerOffVM_Task (commonly invoked via PowerCLI Stop-VM, govc vm.power -off, or scripted SOAP/REST calls)
how_to_implement: Ingest vCenter task/event history or ship hostd.log from every host; alert thresholds should key off VM count within a short window per host or cluster, since bulk actions are the signal, not any single power-off.
known_false_positives: Scheduled maintenance, DR failover tests, cluster-wide patch/reboot orchestration (vSphere Update Manager/lifecycle manager), and UPS-triggered graceful shutdown scripts all power off many VMs quickly; exclude known maintenance-window automation accounts.
investigation_steps: Determine the count and rate of VMs powered off and whether they span multiple hosts/clusters simultaneously.
Identify the initiating account and whether it recently authenticated over SSH or via a new API session.
Check for accompanying snapshot deletion, autostart, firewall, or coredump changes in the same time window - the combination is the real signal.
Check datastore browser / file timestamps for renamed or newly-created ransom-note files (e.g. *.args, *ransom*.html/.txt).

references.title: CISA AA23-039A: ESXiArgs Ransomware Virtual Machine Recovery Guidance

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi Syslog Configuration Changed via ESXCLI
description: Detects use of 'esxcli system syslog config set' to change or remove the remote log host(s) an ESXi host forwards to. Attackers redirect syslog to a host they control, or clear it entirely, so that subsequent destructive actions (snapshot deletion, firewall/coredump disablement, VM power-off) never reach the SOC's SIEM.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal esxcli command line, invoking user, and working directory for every ESXi Shell / SSH session.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: esxcli calls into the same host management daemon and generate a corresponding configuration-change task entry.

data_sources.name: SIEM log-gap monitoring
data_sources.description: The most reliable detection is often the absence of expected heartbeat/log volume from a previously-reporting host - alert on syslog silence, not just the change command.

detection_logic: Alert on any invocation of 'esxcli system syslog config set' that changes --loghost, plus a companion 'no data received from host in N minutes' absence detection for hosts that normally stream continuously - the second catches the case where the attacker's own change event never arrives.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli system syslog config set" "--loghost"
| rex field=_raw "--loghost=(?<new_loghost>\S+)"
| table _time, esxi_host, user, new_loghost, _raw
| append [ | tstats latest(_time) as last_seen from index=esxi by esxi_host | eval minutes_since_last_seen=round((now()-last_seen)/60,1) | where minutes_since_last_seen > 30 ]
cli_reference: esxcli system syslog config set --loghost=<host-or-empty> ; esxcli system syslog reload
how_to_implement: Onboard shell.log and hostd.log via syslog-ng/rsyslog forwarding or the Splunk Add-on for VMware, and build a separate scheduled search that pages on log-volume silence per host so a successful redirect is still caught even if the change event itself is lost.
known_false_positives: Legitimate re-platforming of a syslog collector (SIEM migration, new collector IP) will trigger this; require change-ticket correlation before treating as malicious.
investigation_steps: Compare the new --loghost value against your approved collector inventory.
Check whether the change was followed by a drop in log volume from that host.
Review shell.log/auth.log for the SSH session that issued the command and how it authenticated.
Check for firewall, coredump, and welcome-message changes issued in the same session - they are frequently bundled together.

references.title: Broadcom KB: Configuring syslog on ESXi

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi Welcome Message Changed via ESXCLI
description: Detects use of 'esxcli system welcomemsg set' to overwrite the DCUI/console welcome banner. This is a low-noise but high-fidelity indicator: ransomware crews (ESXiArgs and others) routinely rewrite the welcome message to display the ransom note directly on the host console, and legitimate admins almost never touch this string outside of initial build/branding.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal 'esxcli system welcomemsg set -m="..."' command and its full argument string, which often contains the ransom note text itself.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Corresponding ConfigStore/AdvancedOption update task.

detection_logic: Alert on any invocation of 'esxcli system welcomemsg set'. Given how rarely this is used legitimately, treat every occurrence as an investigate-now event, and raise severity further if the new message contains ransom-note keywords (bitcoin, wallet, decrypt, .onion, restore, tor).
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli system welcomemsg set"
| rex field=_raw "-m=?\"?(?<welcome_message>.*)\"?$"
| eval ransom_keyword_hit=if(match(welcome_message, "(?i)(bitcoin|wallet|decrypt|\.onion|restore|ransom|tor browser)"), 1, 0)
| table _time, esxi_host, user, welcome_message, ransom_keyword_hit
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; this detection needs no CIM mapping or special onboarding beyond raw text search, making it a good early-warning tripwire even in a minimally-instrumented environment.
known_false_positives: Initial host build-out / branding by platform teams (company name, asset tag, support contact) legitimately sets this once during provisioning.
investigation_steps: Read the full new message text for ransom-note or defacement language.
Identify the session/user and whether it authenticated via SSH shortly after SSH was enabled (see the SSH-enable detection).
Check for concurrent snapshot deletion, VM power-off, and firewall/coredump changes.

references.title: Logpoint: ESXiArgs Ransomware analysis

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi VM Snapshots Deleted via VIM-CMD
description: Detects interactive use of 'vim-cmd vmsvc/snapshot.removeall <vmid>' (or 'snapshot.remove') from the ESXi Shell over SSH or the DCUI. This is the command-line twin of the API-based snapshot deletion technique and is the form most commonly seen typed or scripted directly by ransomware operators who have SSH access, including the original ESXiArgs campaign.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Captures the literal 'vim-cmd vmsvc/snapshot.removeall <vmid>' command line, user, and timestamp.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: vim-cmd is a thin wrapper around the same VIM API, so the resulting RemoveSnapshot task still appears here.

detection_logic: Match shell.log command lines containing 'vmsvc/snapshot.removeall' or 'vmsvc/snapshot.remove', and pivot to hostd.log to confirm task completion. Escalate when the same session loops the command across multiple VM IDs in quick succession (commonly done via a one-line for-loop against 'vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms').
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "vim-cmd" ("vmsvc/snapshot.removeall" OR "vmsvc/snapshot.remove")
| rex field=_raw "vmsvc/snapshot\.remove(all)?\s+(?<vmid>\d+)"
| stats count values(vmid) as vmids_targeted by esxi_host, user, ssh_session_id
| where count >= 1
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log to your SIEM; because the command is typed interactively (or piped in via SSH), it is one of the highest-fidelity artifacts of hands-on-keyboard ESXi ransomware activity and should be treated as near-zero false-positive.
known_false_positives: Rare - administrators occasionally clean up orphaned snapshots manually via SSH instead of the vSphere Client; verify against change tickets before dismissing.
investigation_steps: Pull the full shell.log session for the SSH connection (source IP, auth method, prior/following commands).
Check whether SSH was enabled shortly before this session (correlate with the SSH-enable detection).
Determine how many VMs were targeted and whether 'vmsvc/getallvms' was run immediately prior to enumerate targets.
Check for a following 'vmsvc/power.off' loop and firewall/coredump/syslog changes.

references.title: CISA AA23-039A: ESXiArgs Ransomware Virtual Machine Recovery Guidance

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi VM Autostart Disabled via VIM-CMD
description: Detects interactive use of 'vim-cmd hostsvc/autostartmanager/enable_autostart 0' or 'update_autostartentry'/'update_defaults' from the ESXi Shell to turn off automatic VM startup. Ransomware operators disable autostart alongside mass power-off so encrypted/dead VMs do not attempt to relaunch and generate alerts before the extortion note is delivered.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Captures the literal 'vim-cmd hostsvc/autostartmanager/...' command line and session user.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Logs the resulting HostAutoStartManager reconfiguration task.

detection_logic: Match shell.log entries invoking hostsvc/autostartmanager with enable_autostart=0 or update_defaults/update_autostartentry setting startAction to 'none', and correlate with any preceding mass power-off in the same session.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "vim-cmd hostsvc/autostartmanager"
| rex field=_raw "autostartmanager/(?<autostart_action>\S+)"
| table _time, esxi_host, user, autostart_action, _raw
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log for command-line visibility; hostd.log provides task-level corroboration for the same change.
known_false_positives: Host decommissioning, DR-cluster teardown, or lab/test environments toggled by automation may legitimately disable autostart.
investigation_steps: Confirm the session's SSH origin and whether SSH was recently enabled.
Check for accompanying VM power-off or snapshot deletion in the same shell.log session.
Validate against change management for host maintenance.

references.title: VMware Security Blog: ESXi-Targeting Ransomware, Tactics and Techniques

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi Coredump Generation Disabled via ESXCLI
description: Detects use of 'esxcli system coredump partition/file/network set --enable false' to turn off kernel core dump collection. Disabling coredumps removes forensic artifacts that would otherwise capture kernel-level evidence of a compromise, and is commonly bundled with firewall and syslog tampering as part of an ESXi anti-forensics/defense-evasion sequence.

techniques.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal esxcli coredump command line and user.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Corresponding coredump/ConfigStore change task.

detection_logic: Alert on any 'esxcli system coredump partition set --enable false', 'esxcli system coredump file set --enable false', or 'esxcli system coredump network set --enable false' invocation.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli system coredump" "--enable false"
| table _time, esxi_host, user, _raw
cli_reference: esxcli system coredump partition set --enable false  |  esxcli system coredump file set --enable false  |  esxcli system coredump network set --enable false
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; consider a companion configuration-drift check (esxcli system coredump partition get) run on a schedule to catch cases where the enabling command itself wasn't captured.
known_false_positives: Storage teams occasionally disable the coredump partition when reclaiming diagnostic partition space during a boot-disk migration; rare in steady state.
investigation_steps: Identify the session and user, and whether it correlates with syslog or firewall changes.
Check current coredump configuration state (esxcli system coredump partition get) to confirm effect.
Review for subsequent destructive actions (snapshot deletion, mass power-off) in the same session.

references.title: Broadcom KB: Configuring a diagnostic coredump partition on an ESXi host

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi Firewall Disabled via ESXCLI
description: Detects use of 'esxcli network firewall set --enabled false' to turn off the built-in ESXi firewall entirely. This removes ruleset-based restrictions on management-interface services (SSH, VIM API, etc.), widening the host's exposed attack surface and is a common step immediately before or after enabling SSH.

techniques.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal 'esxcli network firewall set --enabled false' command line and user.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Corresponding firewall ConfigStore change task.

detection_logic: Alert on any invocation of 'esxcli network firewall set --enabled false'; treat as high-confidence given how rarely the full firewall (as opposed to a single ruleset) is disabled legitimately.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli network firewall set" "--enabled false"
| table _time, esxi_host, user, _raw
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; pair with a periodic drift check ('esxcli network firewall get') to catch state even if the enabling command line was missed.
known_false_positives: Rare - short-lived troubleshooting by VMware GSS-guided support cases occasionally disables the firewall temporarily; always require change-ticket correlation.
investigation_steps: Identify the session/user and source IP of the SSH connection.
Check whether SSH was enabled in the same or a preceding session.
Review for coredump/syslog tampering and subsequent snapshot deletion or VM power-off.
Re-enable the firewall and rotate credentials for the account used.

references.title: Broadcom TechDocs: Manage the ESXi Firewall

author: Threat Detection Library

title: SSH Enable on ESXi Host via VIM-CMD
description: Detects SSH/Tech Support Mode being turned on via 'vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh' + 'vim-cmd hostsvc/start_ssh' (or the legacy 'enable_remote_tsm'/'start_remote_tsm' equivalents). SSH is disabled by default on ESXi precisely because it is the primary remote command-execution and lateral-movement channel into the hypervisor; enabling it - especially from the DCUI or via automation outside change control - is one of the earliest and highest-value signals in the ESXi ransomware kill chain.

data_sources.name: vobd.log
data_sources.description: Emits the esx.audit.ssh.enabled VOB observation when SSH is turned on for the host - the single most reliable artifact for this technique.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Logs the underlying service-policy/state change task when SSH is enabled/started.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: If enabled via an existing DCUI/local shell session, captures the literal vim-cmd command line.

detection_logic: Alert on any esx.audit.ssh.enabled VOB event or hostd SSH-service-policy change task. Because SSH is off by default and most environments manage it exclusively through change-controlled automation, treat every unscheduled occurrence as a critical, page-now event.
spl:
index=esxi (sourcetype=esxi_vobd "esx.audit.ssh.enabled") OR (sourcetype=esxi_shell_log ("hostsvc/enable_ssh" OR "hostsvc/start_ssh" OR "hostsvc/start_remote_tsm" OR "hostsvc/enable_remote_tsm"))
| table _time, esxi_host, user, sourcetype, _raw
cli_reference: vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh  &&  vim-cmd hostsvc/start_ssh   (legacy: vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_remote_tsm && vim-cmd hostsvc/start_remote_tsm)
how_to_implement: Forward vobd.log and shell.log to your SIEM; alert with no suppression window given how infrequently this should fire. Consider also monitoring the DCUI 'Troubleshooting Options' menu path if console access logging is available.
known_false_positives: Legitimate temporary SSH enablement for VMware Global Support Services troubleshooting, or scripted patch/automation windows that require SSH; both should be tied to a change ticket and a defined auto-disable timer.
investigation_steps: Identify who/what enabled SSH (DCUI console session vs. an existing shell/API session) and from what source.
Check whether an SSH login followed within minutes, and from what source IP.
Review the resulting SSH session's shell.log for snapshot, power, firewall, coredump, or syslog commands.
If unauthorized, disable SSH immediately ('vim-cmd hostsvc/stop_ssh' / 'disable_ssh') and rotate local ESXi account credentials.

references.title: Sygnia: Fire Ant - Hypervisor-Level Espionage Targeting VMware ESXi & vCenter
CISA AA23-039A: ESXiArgs Ransomware Virtual Machine Recovery Guidance

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi VM IDs Enumerated via ESXCLI or VIM-CMD
description: Detects use of 'vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms' or 'esxcli vm process list' to enumerate every registered/running VM and its numeric VMID. This is the reconnaissance step almost every ESXi ransomware encryptor performs first, since the VMID is required as an argument to the subsequent power-off and snapshot-removal commands.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal 'vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms' or 'esxcli vm process list' command line and user.

detection_logic: Match shell.log entries invoking vmsvc/getallvms or 'esxcli vm process list'. Low severity in isolation (routine for admins and monitoring tools), but should feed a sequence-based correlation search that raises severity when followed within minutes by snapshot removal or power-off commands against the enumerated VMIDs.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log ("vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms" OR "esxcli vm process list")
| stats count earliest(_time) as first_seen by esxi_host, user, ssh_session_id
| join type=left ssh_session_id
    [ search index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log ("vmsvc/power.off" OR "vmsvc/snapshot.removeall")
      | stats count as destructive_followup_count by ssh_session_id ]
| eval sequence_alert=if(isnotnull(destructive_followup_count), "Enumeration followed by destructive action - escalate", "Enumeration only")
cli_reference: vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms  |  esxcli vm process list
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; build this as a low-severity 'building block' search feeding a correlation rule rather than a standalone page, to keep noise manageable.
known_false_positives: Extremely common in legitimate admin work, monitoring agents, and backup pre-checks; expect high baseline volume.
investigation_steps: Check whether the enumeration was followed by snapshot deletion or power-off commands against the same VMIDs within the same session.
Identify whether the session is a known monitoring/backup service account.
If followed by destructive commands, treat as an active incident and follow the snapshot/power-off runbooks.

references.title: LOLESXi Project: vim-cmd binary reference

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi System Network Information Enumerated via ESXCLI
description: Detects use of network-enumeration esxcli namespaces such as 'esxcli network ip interface list', 'esxcli network nic list', 'esxcli network ip route ipv4 list', and 'esxcli network vswitch standard list' to map a host's VMkernel interfaces, physical NICs, routing, and virtual switch/portgroup topology. Attackers use this to identify management-interface IPs, additional pivot paths, and other hosts reachable from the compromised ESXi box.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal esxcli network enumeration command lines and user.

detection_logic: Match shell.log entries invoking 'esxcli network ip interface list', 'esxcli network nic list', 'esxcli network ip route ipv4 list', or 'esxcli network vswitch standard list' from an interactive SSH session. Best used as a discovery-stage building block that raises confidence when it co-occurs with other enumeration or the SSH-enable detection in the same session, rather than as a standalone alert.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli network" ("ip interface list" OR "nic list" OR "ip route ipv4 list" OR "vswitch standard list")
| stats count values(_raw) as commands by esxi_host, user, ssh_session_id
cli_reference: esxcli network ip interface list  |  esxcli network nic list  |  esxcli network ip route ipv4 list  |  esxcli network vswitch standard list
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; correlate ssh_session_id across this and other Discovery-tagged detections to build a single reconnaissance timeline per session.
known_false_positives: Very common for legitimate networking troubleshooting and health-check scripts; expect a high baseline and tune thresholds accordingly.
investigation_steps: Review the full session command history for what followed the network enumeration.
Check whether this session also enumerated storage, users, and VMs (a full recon sweep is a stronger indicator than any single command).
Identify the SSH source IP and authentication method.

references.title: Broadcom KB: Identifying and Listing Network Interface Cards (NICs) on VMware ESXi

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi System Information Discovery via VIM-CMD
description: Detects use of 'vim-cmd hostsvc/hostsummary' and related hostsvc namespaces (e.g. 'vimsvc/hostsvc/hostconfig') to pull host build/version, CPU/memory capacity, and registered VM inventory in a single call. Attackers use this to fingerprint the exact ESXi build (for exploit selection) and to size up the environment before staging destructive actions.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal 'vim-cmd hostsvc/hostsummary' (and similar) command line and user.

detection_logic: Match shell.log entries invoking hostsvc/hostsummary or vimsvc/hostsvc/hostconfig. Use as a discovery building-block search; correlate with other enumeration and any subsequent destructive command in the same session for prioritization.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "vim-cmd" ("hostsvc/hostsummary" OR "vimsvc/hostsvc/hostconfig")
| stats count by esxi_host, user, ssh_session_id
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; treat this alongside T1082/T1016/T1087 building blocks feeding a single 'ESXi reconnaissance sweep' correlation search.
known_false_positives: Common in legitimate health-check scripts, monitoring agent polling, and manual troubleshooting.
investigation_steps: Check the full session timeline for a broader recon sweep (network, storage, user, and VM enumeration together).
Identify SSH source IP and whether this session followed SSH being freshly enabled.
Watch for subsequent destructive commands against enumerated VMIDs.

references.title: DPC Virtual Tips: Using the vim-cmd Tool - Practical Guide

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi System Storage Enumerated via ESXCLI
description: Detects use of 'esxcli storage core device list', 'esxcli storage filesystem list', and 'esxcli storage vmfs extent list' to enumerate attached LUNs/datastores and VMFS volumes. Ransomware operators use this to identify every datastore holding .vmdk files worth encrypting, including secondary/backup datastores that might otherwise be missed.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal esxcli storage enumeration command lines and user.

detection_logic: Match shell.log entries invoking 'esxcli storage core device list', 'esxcli storage filesystem list', or 'esxcli storage vmfs extent list'. Use as a discovery building-block; correlate with VM enumeration and later encryption/deletion activity for prioritization.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli storage" ("core device list" OR "filesystem list" OR "vmfs extent list")
| stats count values(_raw) as commands by esxi_host, user, ssh_session_id
cli_reference: esxcli storage core device list  |  esxcli storage filesystem list  |  esxcli storage vmfs extent list
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; correlate ssh_session_id with VM-enumeration and destructive-action detections to build a full attack timeline.
known_false_positives: Common for legitimate storage troubleshooting, capacity reporting scripts, and backup software pre-checks.
investigation_steps: Review the full session for a broader recon sweep across network, VM, user, and storage enumeration.
Check for subsequent snapshot deletion or datastore file modification.
Identify SSH source IP and authentication method.

title: ESXi System Users Enumerated via ESXCLI
description: Detects use of 'esxcli system account list' and 'esxcli system permission list' to enumerate local ESXi accounts and their assigned roles/privileges. Attackers use this to find additional accounts to target for credential theft or persistence, and to confirm the privilege level of the session they already control.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal 'esxcli system account list' / 'esxcli system permission list' command line and user.

detection_logic: Match shell.log entries invoking 'esxcli system account list' or 'esxcli system permission list'. Use as a discovery building-block; escalate when it co-occurs with SSH-enable or with a newly-created account shortly afterward.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli system" ("account list" OR "permission list")
| stats count values(_raw) as commands by esxi_host, user, ssh_session_id
cli_reference: esxcli system account list  |  esxcli system permission list
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; join against a subsequent 'esxcli system account add' event to catch enumerate-then-persist sequences.
known_false_positives: Routine for identity/access audits and compliance scans (e.g. CIS benchmark automation).
investigation_steps: Check whether a new local account was created shortly after this enumeration.
Review the full session for a broader recon sweep.
Identify SSH source IP and authentication method.

title: ESXi Firewall Default Action Set to Pass
description: Detects use of 'esxcli network firewall set --default-action true' to flip the ESXi firewall's default policy from deny (DROP) to allow (PASS). Unlike fully disabling the firewall, this is a subtler change that keeps the firewall service 'enabled' in status output while effectively permitting all traffic that isn't explicitly blocked - an evasion technique that can slip past a shallow 'is the firewall on?' check.

techniques.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal 'esxcli network firewall set --default-action true' command line and user.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Corresponding firewall ConfigStore change task.

detection_logic: Alert on any 'esxcli network firewall set' invocation containing '--default-action true'. Because the default action ships as DROP/false, any flip to PASS/true should be treated as high-confidence tampering.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli network firewall set" "--default-action true"
| table _time, esxi_host, user, _raw
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; pair with a scheduled drift check ('esxcli network firewall get') that flags Default Action = true wherever your baseline expects false.
known_false_positives: Rare, typically only seen during vendor-directed troubleshooting for a specific connectivity issue; should always be time-boxed and ticketed.
investigation_steps: Identify the session/user and whether SSH was recently enabled.
Check current firewall state with 'esxcli network firewall get' to confirm effective policy.
Review for concurrent ruleset changes or the full-disable variant of this technique.
Revert the default action to false and audit exposed services.

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi VM Powered Off via VIM-CMD
description: Detects interactive use of 'vim-cmd vmsvc/power.off <vmid>' from the ESXi Shell to power off one or more VMs, releasing the .vmdk file locks the running VMX process holds. This is the command-line form of the API-based power-off technique and, when looped across every enumerated VMID, is one of the clearest hands-on-keyboard signals of imminent ESXi ransomware encryption.

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Captures the literal 'vim-cmd vmsvc/power.off <vmid>' command line, user, and timestamp for every invocation, including looped/scripted sequences.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: Corresponding PowerOffVM_Task creation/completion for each VMID.

detection_logic: Match shell.log entries invoking 'vmsvc/power.off', and alert with elevated severity when the same session issues it against multiple distinct VMIDs in a short window (a for-loop pattern is common: 'for id in $(vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms | ...); do vim-cmd vmsvc/power.off $id; done').
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "vim-cmd vmsvc/power.off"
| rex field=_raw "vmsvc/power\.off\s+(?<vmid>\d+)"
| stats count dc(vmid) as distinct_vms values(vmid) as vmids by esxi_host, user, ssh_session_id
| where distinct_vms >= 5
| eval alert="Scripted mass VM power-off via vim-cmd - possible ransomware staging"
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; this is a near-zero false-positive artifact for bulk usage and should page immediately when the distinct-VMID threshold is crossed within a single session.
known_false_positives: Manual single-VM shutdown by an admin working directly on the console during break/fix; bulk usage across many VMs is rarely legitimate outside a documented maintenance window.
investigation_steps: Pull the full shell.log session and identify preceding 'vmsvc/getallvms' enumeration.
Determine SSH source IP, auth method, and whether SSH was recently enabled.
Check for immediately-following snapshot removal and autostart-disable commands in the same session.
Check datastore file timestamps for signs of active or completed encryption.

author: Threat Detection Library

title: ESXi VIB Acceptance Level Set to Community Supported via ESXCLI
description: Detects use of 'esxcli software acceptance set --level=CommunitySupported' to lower the host's VIB (vSphere Installation Bundle) acceptance level from its default (PartnerSupported or higher) to the least-trusted tier. CommunitySupported VIBs are unsigned and undergo no VMware or partner validation; lowering to this level is a documented precursor step attackers use to install malicious/backdoored VIBs (as seen in the real-world VirtualPita/VirtualPie/VirtualGate ESXi implants) that survive host reboots and evade guest-level EDR entirely.

techniques.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

data_sources.name: shell.log
data_sources.description: Records the literal 'esxcli software acceptance set --level=CommunitySupported' command line and user.

data_sources.name: hostd.log
data_sources.description: esximage acceptance-level change task, and subsequent VIB install (esxcli software vib install) tasks that would otherwise be rejected at a stricter level.

detection_logic: Alert on any 'esxcli software acceptance set' invocation where --level equals CommunitySupported, and escalate severity further if a 'esxcli software vib install' with --force or --no-sig-check follows in the same session.
spl:
index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli software acceptance set" "CommunitySupported"
| table _time, esxi_host, user, _raw
| append
    [ search index=esxi sourcetype=esxi_shell_log "esxcli software vib install" ("--no-sig-check" OR "--force")
      | table _time, esxi_host, user, _raw ]
| sort _time
how_to_implement: Forward shell.log; add a scheduled drift check ('esxcli software acceptance get') alerting whenever the level differs from your organization's approved baseline (typically PartnerSupported or VMwareAccepted).
known_false_positives: Legitimate installation of certain community/open-source VIBs (e.g. some hardware vendor drivers, homelab tooling) requires this level; should be rare and change-ticketed in production/enterprise environments.
investigation_steps: Check current acceptance level ('esxcli software acceptance get') and full VIB list ('esxcli software vib list') for anything unsigned or unexpected installed after the change.
Review shell.log for a following 'esxcli software vib install' command and inspect the source of the VIB (local file vs. remote URL).
If an unexpected VIB was installed, treat the host as compromised: capture forensic images before remediation and rebuild/reinstall ESXi rather than trusting in-place removal.
Restore the acceptance level to your approved baseline.
